summaries.example: Imagine a weather report says it will rain tomorrow. Does that mean rain must happen, no matter what anyone does? A fatalist argument may say yes. But one reply is that a future event can be open: the statement may not yet be simply true or false. What people do, such as carrying an umbrella or changing plans, may be part of how the future unfolds.
summaries.summary: Fatalism is the idea that no one has the power to do anything except what actually happens. The entry examines arguments for this idea, especially an argument connected with Aristotle. Suppose one person says a sea-battle will happen in the future and another says it will not. Since one claim seems true and the other false, the argument tries to say that the event was already unavoidable. Critics focus on the step from truth to necessity. Aristotle’s main reply is that claims about events that are not settled may be neither true nor false yet. Other philosophers keep ordinary ideas about truth but question how the past, the future, time, or human power work. The entry also discusses theological fatalism: the concern that an all-knowing God’s earlier knowledge might make later choices unable to be different. Several possible replies are considered, and no single solution is presented as finally established.
key_ideas: A famous argument linked with Aristotle starts from claims about future events and tries to conclude that everything must happen.
The important step is the move from a statement being true to the event being unavoidable. Philosophers disagree about whether that move works.
One reply says that some future claims are not yet true or false. Other replies explain truth, time, or ability in different ways.
Fatalism is not the same as the idea that events have causes. The entry focuses mainly on arguments from logic and, later, from divine knowledge.
The so-called Idle Argument says effort would be useless, but a reply is that an action can be part of the way an event happens.
summaries.why_it_matters: These arguments affect how we think about choice, planning, responsibility, truth, and time. They also show why a conclusion can seem obvious while depending on a hidden idea, such as “every claim must already be true or false.” Studying fatalism helps us examine arguments carefully rather than assuming that a prediction or a piece of knowledge automatically removes our ability to act.

important_terms.definition: The view that people cannot do anything other than what they actually do.
Something that cannot happen otherwise; in this entry, it often means that nothing can prevent it.
A sentence or claim that is either true or false. Some philosophers question whether this applies to every claim about the open future.
A claim about a future event that is not certain to happen and is not impossible.

questions_to_think_about: If a prediction comes true, was the event unavoidable when the prediction was made?
Can a choice help cause a future event even if that event is certain to happen?
Should every sentence about tomorrow already be true or false?
Why might it matter whether the future is already real?

summaries.example: Suppose that in 1900 someone truthfully said, “A sea-battle will occur on January 1, 2100.” A fatalist argument reasons that, because the statement was already true, the battle was already necessary: nothing could have prevented it. The disputed point is not whether the sentence is true in the end, but whether its truth in 1900 made the later event unavoidable. An alternative view treats the future event as contingent and denies that the earlier statement had a settled truth-value at that time.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry examines philosophical arguments that conclude we are powerless to do otherwise. Its central case is logical fatalism. In Aristotle’s example, either a future sea-battle will occur or it will not; if one of the corresponding propositions must already be true, the argument seems to make the event necessary from every earlier time. The pressure point is the truth-to-necessity link. Aristotle is presented as offering a solution in which future-contingent propositions lack a settled truth-value, although this challenges standard assumptions about bivalence, negation, and truth-functional connectives. Related approaches retain bivalence by revising the analysis of tense, truth, or reference time, or by rejecting the idea that a statement is made true by the world’s state at the time of utterance. The entry then considers the necessity of the past, Taylor’s argument about power, and objections concerning what counts as a necessary condition for action. It also treats theological fatalism: if God’s infallible knowledge precedes an action, does the agent still have the power to refrain? Aristotelian, Ockhamist, Boethian, and other proposals are assessed without a final endorsement. Middle knowledge creates a further problem because it concerns what free creatures would do in possible circumstances. Finally, the Idle Argument is criticized for overlooking the possibility that deliberation and action help produce the outcome.
key_ideas: Aristotle’s sea-battle argument appears to derive inevitability from the truth or falsity of opposing predictions. Its crucial transition is from truth to necessity.

On the Aristotelian solution, a future-contingent claim may be neither true nor false before the event is settled. This preserves an open future but creates difficulties for familiar logical rules and ordinary judgments about predictions.

Other responses reject the relevant theory of truth, distinguish truth at a time from truth without qualification, or locate the truth-making facts at the event’s time rather than the utterance’s time.

Arguments from the necessity of the past and Richard Taylor’s account of the conditions of power provide different routes to fatalism. Critics challenge whether all past-directed propositions are necessary and whether lacking a necessary condition always removes an agent’s power.

Theological fatalism asks whether God’s prior infallible knowledge prevents human freedom. Proposed responses include an Aristotelian treatment of future contingents, Ockham’s distinction between hard and soft facts about the past, timeless divine knowledge, and revisions of what omniscience involves.

The Idle Argument claims deliberation is pointless, but the relevant reply is that an action may be necessary as part of the route to an outcome. The entry concludes that fatalism and the Aristotelian solution might both be wrong, though the issue remains open.
summaries.why_it_matters: Fatalism connects abstract questions in logic and metaphysics with practical ideas about deliberation, agency, and responsibility. It also illustrates how debates about time and truth shape debates about freedom. The entry is valuable because it does not treat one argument as decisive: it identifies the assumptions behind several arguments and shows that rejecting fatalism may require accepting difficult claims about truth, time, the past, or knowledge.

important_terms.definition: The thesis that agents lack the power to do anything other than what they in fact do. Philosophical discussions distinguish arguments for it from mere resignation.
In this context, inevitability: at a time, nothing can prevent an event from occurring. This differs from logical necessity.
The principle that every proposition is either true or false. Aristotle’s proposed response questions this for some future contingents.
A proposition about a future event that is neither necessary nor impossible, such as a genuinely unsettled future occurrence.
The view that a proposition is true because reality, in an appropriate way, corresponds to what it says.
A view of time on which past, present, and future are understood through their relations to a reference time, with all times typically treated as equally real.
A family of views on which being past, present, or future involves more than a relation to a reference time; some versions treat the future as not yet real.
The problem of whether divine, infallible knowledge of future actions is compatible with an agent’s power to do otherwise.

questions_to_think_about: Does the truth of a future-tense proposition entail that the event is unavoidable, or does that depend on a theory of truth and time?
Can a proposition about the past partly depend on a future event without making the past changeable?
What condition must be added to the claim that an agent cannot act when a necessary condition is absent?
Would timeless divine knowledge avoid the problem of foreknowledge and freedom, or would similar concerns return?
Why does the Idle Argument confuse an action being involved in an outcome with an action being irrelevant to it?

summaries.example: Your friend says, “You will choose the blue project for science class.” Later, you do choose it. Does your friend’s correct prediction show that you could not have chosen red? Fatalism says that arguments may lead toward that conclusion. But the prediction might have been true because you freely chose blue, not because the choice was forced. Philosophers ask whether the prediction’s truth made your choice unavoidable or merely described what happened.
summaries.summary: Fatalism is the philosophical view that people are unable to do anything other than what they actually do. The entry begins with a famous argument associated with Aristotle. If a future event will happen or will not happen, then one of two opposing statements seems true. The argument tries to move from that fact to the conclusion that the event was unavoidable from the beginning. Critics question this move, especially the assumption that a statement’s truth at an earlier time makes the event necessary. Aristotle’s proposed answer is that some statements about future events that are not settled are neither true nor false yet. This is called rejecting bivalence in those cases. It avoids fatalism but creates puzzles about how words such as “or” and “not” work. Other responses distinguish different kinds of truth, different times, or different theories of time. The entry also considers arguments saying the past is necessary, and arguments about whether lacking a condition for an action removes an agent’s power. Theological fatalism applies the issue to God’s foreknowledge. Philosophers discuss whether God might be timeless, whether divine knowledge is like ordinary belief, or whether omniscience must include every future fact. The discussion ends by noting that several arguments for fatalism can be challenged, but that no simple answer settles every issue.
key_ideas: The classic argument uses two opposite claims about a future event: one must seem to be true, and the other false. It then tries to infer that the future was fixed all along.
The argument’s most controversial step is treating truth as proof of inevitability. A true prediction does not obviously show that the event could not have happened differently.
Aristotle’s main solution is that a claim about an unsettled future may be neither true nor false before the event occurs. This protects an open future but makes ordinary logic more complicated.
Other philosophers keep the idea that every claim is true or false but change how they understand tense, time, or what makes a statement true.
The same question appears in religious form: if God already knows what someone will do, can that person still have the power to do something else?
The Idle Argument says there is no point in taking action if the outcome is already fated. A reply says that the action may be part of the cause of the outcome.
summaries.why_it_matters: Fatalism helps us investigate whether planning and choosing make a real difference. It also teaches an important reasoning skill: identify the extra assumption that connects one claim to a surprising conclusion. Questions about future truth, time, past events, and divine knowledge can change how we understand freedom, even when the debate begins with a simple sentence about what will happen.

important_terms.definition: The view that no one can do anything except what they actually do, so alternatives are not genuinely within their power.
Being unable to happen otherwise. In fatalist arguments, this often means that no one could prevent the event.
The rule that every claim is either true or false. Some philosophers reject this rule for unsettled claims about the future.
A future event that could happen but could also fail to happen; it is not already required or ruled out.
The idea that a statement is true when reality makes it match what the statement says.
The view that future events are not yet fully settled or real in the same way as past and present events.
The view that past, present, and future are mainly positions in a time order, with times often understood as equally real.
The challenge that God’s infallible knowledge of a future action might leave a person unable to choose differently.

questions_to_think_about: Does a correct prediction remove a person’s freedom, or can it simply report a free choice?
Should a claim about an uncertain future be called true before the event happens?
How could a statement about the past partly concern the future?
Can a doctor’s advice matter if recovery is certain?
What is the difference between something being impossible and someone lacking the power to make it happen?
